MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "a stiff THA with bone in the soft tissues — what is it?"
- "It is **heterotopic ossification (HO)**, graded **Brooker I–IV**."
- "Grades **III–IV** bring pain and stiffness."
- "Prevent it in high-risk hips with an **NSAID** or one **radiation** dose; excise it only when **mature**."

### Definition and Brooker Classification
HO is new bone in the soft tissues around the hip; Brooker grades it by the gap between the spurs.

#### Definition
- HO ranges from a faint density to complete bony **ankylosis**
- Calcification shows on the film by **3–4 weeks**
- The bone takes **1–2 years** to mature fully (Campbell)
- Most patients have no symptoms; grades III–IV limit motion and hurt

#### Brooker Classification

| Brooker grade (Campbell) | What the film shows |
|---|---|
| **I** | bone islands in the soft tissue |
| **II** | spurs, gap **≥1 cm** |
| **III** | spurs, gap **<1 cm** |
| **IV** | **ankylosis** |

MEMORY HOOK — the 1 cm ruler
- Brooker carries a 1 cm ruler: it fits the gap in **II**, not in **III**; **IV** is fused.

[[FIG: Fig 17.1 · 17.1

### Risk Factors
The grade tells you how bad it is; the risk list tells you whom to protect.

#### Patient Factors
- High-risk patients are men with **hypertrophic OA** (osteoarthritis)
- **Ankylosing spondylitis** and **DISH** carry the same risk
- DISH = diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
- A patient with **previous HO** is high risk too
- **Paget disease** and African American ethnicity complete the list

#### Surgical Approach
- The approach changes where HO forms: in the abductors or in the rotators
- Anterior and anterolateral approaches involve the **anterior abductors**
- The posterior approach involves the short rotators, iliopsoas and posterior abductors
- With the DAA (direct anterior approach), HO is **almost zero** (Prof Sherif Khaled)

### Prevention
Prophylaxis works only before the bone forms, so it starts around the operation.

#### Indications for Prophylaxis
- Give prophylaxis to **high-risk patients only**
- Both routes act on precursor cells only, so formed bone can only be removed

#### Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs
- **Indomethacin** 25 mg three times daily, for up to 6 weeks (Surgery of the Hip)
- Courses of **7 days** also work (Campbell); the Handbook gives 10–14 days
- COX-2 inhibitors are equally effective and safer, so they are now preferred
- Aspirin given against VTE (venous thromboembolism) also reduces HO
- Compliance is limited by side effects and contraindications

#### Radiation Therapy
- A **single** dose of **6–8 Gy** (Miller); doses as low as **5 Gy** work
- It fails more often if given **>8 h** before or **>72 h** after surgery (Campbell)
- A preoperative dose is more comfortable than an early postoperative one
- The field covers only the soft tissue around the hip
- **Shield** the ingrowth surfaces of the implants

PITFALL — the radiation window
- Miller: ≤24 h before or ≤72 h after; Campbell: failures beyond **8 h** before or **72 h** after.
- Say → "**One low dose, within hours before or ≤72 h after** surgery, implant surfaces shielded."

### Excision of Mature Heterotopic Bone
Once the bone has formed, the only answer is to cut it out, and timing is everything.

#### Indications
- Excision is **rarely** needed, because the pain is usually mild
- It needs an extensile exposure, and the bone hides the landmarks
- Expect **heavy blood loss**

#### Timing and Maturity
- Excise only **mature** bone, at ≥**6 months** (Miller)
- The Handbook waits 6 months to 1 year
- Maturity = falling activity on the bone scan and a **normal alkaline phosphatase**
- Immature bone bleeds and recurs
- Newer view (Handbook): symptomatic HO may be excised earlier; the classic answer still waits

#### Outcome
- Give prophylaxis again with the excision: radiation or an NSAID
- Motion improves, but pain may persist

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Brooker by the 1 cm gap · NSAID or 6–8 Gy early · excise at 6 months**

17.2.b:
HO is bone where we did not want it; the trochanter is bone we cut on purpose and then need to heal.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when do you cut the trochanter, and how do you fix it?"
- "Cut it for an **extensile exposure**, or to **transfer** it for abductor tension."
- "An **ETO** (extended trochanteric osteotomy) runs ≥**10 cm** from the trochanter tip."
- "Fix it rigidly with **≥2–3 cables** or a claw plate; never with sutures alone."

### Indications
The osteotomy does two jobs: it opens the femur, or it moves the abductors.

#### Exposure
- An **extensile approach** in revision
[[FIG: Fig 17.2 · 17.2
- To remove a well-fixed cement mantle or stem
- Ankylosis, HO and malposition also need the room
- It also gives exposure in the anterolateral (Watson-Jones) approach

#### Trochanteric Transfer
- Transfer means **advancement**: the trochanter moves inferolaterally
- It gives **more abductor tension**
- Dysplasia: the abductors are weak before surgery
- Protrusio: the medial head brings the trochanter near the ilium, so the abductors are slack
- Recurrent dislocation from **lax soft tissue**, not malposition: advance instead of revising
- A fused hip converted to THA: the inactive abductors need routine advancement
- A shortened femur: distal advancement restores abductor tension

#### Extended Trochanteric Osteotomy
- It removes the **lateral third** of the femur, the "coffin lid", for straight access to the canal
- Cement in a **varus** femur: the ETO allows neutral reaming
[[FIG: Fig 17.3 · 17.2
- Other uses: a long cement mantle in infection, or a well-fixed cementless stem
- It also removes a nail, corrects proximal deformity and improves acetabular exposure
- It lets hardware out and resets abductor tension

#### Indications by Frequency
- Paprosky (2018): **infection** first, then Vancouver **B2** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Then femoral loosening; a varus femur comes last

#### Contraindication
- **Cemented femoral revision**: cement enters the cut and spoils fixation
- So the ETO is used only when a **cementless** stem is planned
- Some authors worry about its non-union rate

#### Advantages
- It is versatile and makes cement removal, the dangerous stage, much safer
- It shortens surgery and lowers blood loss, perforation and fracture
- It starts as a window but becomes an extensile exposure

### Types of Trochanteric Osteotomy
Three cuts differ by the muscles left on the fragment.
[[FIG: Fig 17.4 · 17.2

#### Standard Osteotomy
- It carries **gluteus medius** only
- It starts just below the vastus tubercle, 45° proximally and medially, sparing the neck
- It gives the best view of the ilium for big acetabular revisions

#### Trochanteric Slide
- In a slide, vastus lateralis stays attached to the fragment
- So it counters the abductor pull
- Migration >1 cm occurs in only **11%** of its non-unions, with less limp (Campbell)

#### Extended Trochanteric Osteotomy
- A long lateral cortical segment is raised with the trochanter
- An extended osteotomy is ≈10–12 cm, one-third of the circumference (Handbook)
- Its long contact surface resists the abductor pull and takes more fixation

#### Approach Matters
- In the modified McFarland, medius and vastus lateralis stay one sleeve
- So the ETO fragment remains a **muscle flap**, never a loose piece
- Registry data: the lateral approach with a trochanteric osteotomy had the best long-term survival
- An osteotomy did not reduce abductor strength

### Preoperative Planning of Extended Trochanteric Osteotomy
Templating decides the cut, so know its length before the knife.

#### Osteotomy Length
- Plan it ≥**10 cm** from the GT (greater trochanter) tip (Prof Abdel Karim)
[[FIG: Fig 17.5 · 17.2
- Then add **4–6 cm** of diaphyseal fit for the stem
- Campbell keeps **5–6 cm** of isthmus contact
- So the cut is usually 12–16 cm long
- There is no fixed number: take it from templating and the company's sizes
- Confirm the length with an image in theatre, especially for a long stem

#### Common Errors
- Too short, too long, or no room left for the stem
[[FIG: Fig 17.6 · 17.2
- A proximal fracture, or failure to remove the implant
- With a femoral deformity, make the osteotomy **at the apex**

#### Sequence and Backup
- Do the ETO **before dislocation** in a stiff, subsided or protruded hip
- Otherwise dislocation can fracture the femur
- Never start without **backup** implants

MEMORY HOOK — the trapdoor
- An ETO is a trapdoor: **10 cm** long at least, with **4–6 cm** of solid bone below for the stem.

### Surgical Technique of Extended Trochanteric Osteotomy
The cut is planned on film; in theatre, the details prevent the fracture.

#### Exposure
- Prof Abdel Karim prefers the **posterior approach**
[[FIG: Fig 17.7 · 17.2
- Lateral and anterolateral routes also work
- Anterior surgeons must be able to convert
- Trans-trochanteric approaches gave the best exposure in every domain; posterior came next
- Keep the sleeve: gluteus medius above, vastus lateralis below
- Strip only ≈2 cm for a Hohmann retractor

#### Marking
- Measure the length from the template, usually 12–16 cm
[[FIG: Fig 17.8 · 17.2
- Mark it with methylene blue or diathermy

#### Posterior Limb
- An experienced surgeon cuts with the saw
- Otherwise, **drill holes** first, so the saw does not deflect
- Add one hole at the corner against comminution
- **Round** the corners with a pencil burr; a square corner fractures

#### Anterior Limb
- Complete it with a saw or burr, minding the anterior vessels
[[FIG: Fig 17.9 · 17.2
- Or make a controlled fracture through drill holes
- The fragment is one-third of the circumference
- Do not strip vastus lateralis, so the fragment keeps its blood supply

#### Levering the Fragment
- Insert **2–3 osteotomes** and lever gently
[[FIG: Fig 17.10 · 17.2
- First release the **anterior pseudocapsule**, or the fragment breaks
- How a careless ETO fractures the femur → 15 Periprosthetic fractures

#### Stem Extraction
- Free a cementless stem with a Gigli saw down its medial side
- Flexible and back-cutting osteotomes help

### Fixation
A cut trochanter must be held rigidly, because the abductors pull on it with every step.

#### Prophylactic Distal Cerclage
- Place a cable **below the osteotomy before reaming**, so the femur does not split
- Its details → 15 Periprosthetic fractures

#### Cables and Wires
- **Rigid fixation** with ≥2–3 cables or wires
[[FIG: Fig 17.11 · 17.2
- Distal cable first, then 2–3 proximally
- Without cables, use a double-wire cerclage
- A **claw or cable-grip plate** with cables hooks over the tip and holds around it

#### Reattachment
- Abduct the hip **≤10–15°** while reattaching (Campbell)
- Reduce it anatomically or slightly distally, with **compression**
- Superior or medial tilt leads to non-union

#### Trochanteric Advancement
- Remove a block distally and slide the fragment down
[[FIG: Fig 17.12 · 17.2
- It tensions the abductors

#### Case
- An infected THA had a well-fixed stem, so an ETO was needed
[[FIG: Fig 17.13 · 17.2
- It was closed with **triple cerclage**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the cut trochanter has not united — so what?"
- "Non-union follows **3–8%** of primaries and **9–13%** of revisions."
- "**Migration >2 cm** weakens the abductors and raises dislocation."
- "Prevent it with a large fragment, **rigid cables**, a brace and no resisted abduction."

### Incidence and Significance
A stable fibrous union is harmless; a migrated fragment is not.

#### Incidence
- Non-union follows **3–8%** of primaries (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 17.14 · 17.3
- It follows **9–13%** of revisions
- The Handbook quotes 2–15%; wiring techniques reach **25%**

#### Significance
- Fibrous union without migration gives little pain and good function
- Migration >**2 cm** makes the abductors fail, even if it unites
- Displaced non-union raises dislocation: **17.6%** vs 2.8% (Campbell)

### Risk Factors
Most non-unions come from the fragment, the fixation or the patient.
- A small fragment and **poor bone**
- Weak fixation and excess abductor tension
- Prior radiation and a noncompliant patient
- Failure starts with to-and-fro motion in flexion, rising from a chair or on stairs
- Fixation then fatigues, and only then does the fragment migrate

### Prevention
Prevention starts before the cut and ends months later.

#### Bone and Fragment
- Good bone and a **large fragment**; osteoporotic bone should not be osteotomised
- A transferred trochanter needs a refreshed bed
- A trochanter fixed back in place needs pre-drilling before the cut

#### Fixation
- Never **suture alone**, because it may not unite
- Union is likelier with a slide, cables around the femur and good bone contact

PITFALL — wires or a plate?
- Handbook: screws or a plate, as wires and cerclage are weak; Prof Abdel Karim, Campbell: cables and wires.
- Say → "**≥2–3 cables, or a claw plate with cables**; wire alone fails for a non-union."

#### After Surgery
- **Delayed weight bearing** and an abduction brace
- Delay full weight bearing 4–6 weeks if fixation is not rigid
- No active resisted abduction

### Management
Treat the pain, the hardware or the pseudarthrosis, whichever is the cause.

#### Hardware Problems
- Broken or prominent hardware causes lateral hip pain
- A local anaesthetic injection confirms it; removal of wire relieves <50%
- Broken wires or cables fret, and fragments in the joint cause **third-body wear**
- Remove braided cables that fret, because their debris speeds wear and osteolysis
- Migrated wires can compress the sciatic nerve later

#### Proximal Migration
- Against proximal migration, the slide keeps vastus lateralis as a tether
- A tight anterior pseudocapsule is released

#### Repair of the Pseudarthrosis
- Indications: a painful pseudarthrosis or a Trendelenburg limp
- Clues: pain on resisted abduction, local tenderness, relief by injection
- Wire alone fails; a crossover wire with a spring united **81%** (Campbell)
- A claw plate with wires united 51 of 72; add bone graft, never tension

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "foot drop after THA — what do you do?"
- "It is a **sciatic** palsy, mostly its **peroneal division**: stretch, retractor, haematoma or lengthening."
- "Look for a **haematoma** or dislocation: evacuate or reduce it."
- "Shorten an overlengthened leg, then EMG and a splint."

### Incidence and Nerves at Risk
A palsy follows about one hip in a hundred.

#### Incidence
- Nerve injury follows ≈**1%** of THAs (Prof Fawzy)
[[FIG: Fig 17.15 · 17.4
- Campbell: **0.5%** primary, **2.3%** dysplasia, **3.5%** revision

#### Nerves at Risk by Approach
- The **sciatic** nerve is commonest
- Then the femoral, superior gluteal and obturator nerves

| Approach | Nerve at risk |
|---|---|
| Posterior | **sciatic** |
| Lateral | **superior gluteal** |
| Anterior | **lateral femoral cutaneous** |

### Mechanisms and Risk Factors
Laceration is rare; most nerves are squeezed or stretched.

| Mechanism (common) | Who is at risk |

MEMORY HOOK — the dog on a short leash
- The peroneal division is a dog on a short leash: tied at the notch, little fat, it takes the full pull.

#### Limb Lengthening
- Some series found no link with lengthening, so they blamed mechanical trauma
- A shorter modular head has reversed a palsy

PITFALL — how much lengthening is safe?
- Prof Fawzy: risk **>2.5 cm**; Prof Zamel allows 3.5–4 cm in dysplasia.
- Campbell: peroneal palsy at 1.9–3.7 cm, sciatic at 4–5.1 cm.
- Say → "Risk rises past **≈2.5 cm**; in dysplasia, palpate the nerve as the leg comes down."

### Other Nerves
The sciatic nerve dominates, but each approach has its own nerve.

#### Femoral Nerve
- It lies in front of the capsule, separated only by iliopsoas
- A retractor anterior to iliopsoas injures it
- Palsy follows **0.21%** of THAs, ×14.8 with anterior approaches (Campbell)
- Recovery starts after 6 months; 75% recover fully; brace the knee meanwhile
- In the DAA, a retractor under iliocapsularis protects it
- An obese patient with a short neck and protrusio took 1 year to recover

#### Superior Gluteal Nerve
- Its neuropraxia causes a **Trendelenburg gait**
- Stay in the medius–minimus plane, with no excess traction
- Its course and the 5 cm split → 13 Instability

#### Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve
- It is the DAA's nerve: open the fascia over the TFL belly, laterally
- Injury is reported in up to **81%** of DAAs (Campbell)
- It is usually transient, ≈12 weeks (Prof Abo Elsoud)

#### Obturator Nerve
- Extruded cement, retractors and anteroinferior screws injure it
- Persistent **groin pain** may be its only sign

### Diagnosis
The first job is to find a cause you can still reverse.
- A new palsy with a tense, painful thigh means **haematoma**, often on anticoagulants
- Urgent decompression can reverse it
- Record sciatic function before any reduction
- **EMG** shows the level and the recovery

### Management
Treat the cause first, then support the limb while it recovers.

| Finding | What to do |
|---|---|
| Foot drop | **splint** |
| Haematoma | **evacuate** |
| Dislocation | **reduce** |
| Overlengthened leg | **shorten** |
| Persistent palsy | **explore** |

#### Late Exploration
- Explore if there is no recovery at **6 weeks**, or compression is suspected (Campbell)
- CT shows the site of impingement

#### Outcome
- Recovery: good **40%**, mild **45%**, severe **15%** (Prof Fawzy)
- Campbell: complete recovery in only 20–50% beyond 1 year
- It can take up to 2–3 years
- In axonotmesis the nerve regrows ≈**1 mm/day**

17.5.b:
Vessel injury is rarer than nerve injury, and its bleeding may stay hidden.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the BP falls during a revision cup — what happened?"
- "Think of a **vessel injury**: **0.2%** of revisions, **0.04%** of primaries."
- "Retractors, screws and over-reaming are the causes."
- "Control, transfuse and pack, then call the **vascular surgeon**."

### Incidence and Vessels at Risk
Four vessel groups lie close to the acetabulum.
- It follows **0.2%** of revisions and **0.04%** of primaries (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 17.17 · 17.5
- Prof Fawzy quotes 0.2–0.3% overall
- Mortality is **7–9%**, amputation 15%, permanent disability 17% (Campbell)
- The iliac, femoral, superior gluteal and obturator vessels are at risk

### Mechanisms and Risk Factors
Most injuries come from our own instruments or screws.

| Mechanism | Who is at risk |
|---|---|
| sharp or blunt instruments (retractors) | **revision**, dysplasia |
| screws through the acetabulum | **atherosclerosis**, previous vascular surgery |

#### Instruments and Implants
- Sharp: knife and osteotomes
- Blunt: retractors compress, stretch or tear a vessel
- Cables, cages, threaded cups and grafts can also injure it
- Intrapelvic migration of components is a risk factor

#### Cement and Late Damage
- **Over-reaming** lets cement through the floor
[[FIG: Fig 17.18 · 17.5
- Its heat causes **thrombosis**
- Late erosion forms a **pseudoaneurysm**
- Extruded cement may spare the vessels and still irritate the obturator nerve

#### Acetabular Screws
- Posterosuperior screws are safe; posteroinferior screws ≤**20 mm**
- Even in the safe zone, the superior gluteal vessels lie close, so keep inside the lines
- Palpate the drill tip through the sciatic notch
- The anterior quadrants hold the iliac and obturator vessels, so avoid them
- The full quadrant system → 02 Fixation

MEMORY HOOK — the burglar's route
- Screw like a burglar: in through the back window, upstairs (posterosuperior); the front door is guarded by the iliac vessels.

### Diagnosis and Management
Bleeding may be hidden, so watch the numbers, not only the wound.

| Recognise | Treat |
|---|---|
| occult bleeding: BP falls, HR rises | control the bleeding, transfuse, pack |
| or limb ischaemia, so stay alert | call the **vascular surgeon**; angiography afterwards |

#### Intraoperative Bleeding
- Call the vascular surgeon or an **interventional radiologist** at once
- Retroperitoneal exposure allows a temporary clamp on the iliac vessels
- Embolisation can control pelvic bleeding

#### Late Vascular Lesions
- Iliac thrombosis, an AV (arteriovenous) fistula or a **false aneurysm**
- False aneurysm follows infection, migrated threaded cups and pointed retractors
- Suspect it with persistent wound bleeding or a **pulsatile mass**

### Prevention
Most vascular injuries are avoided by where we put our retractors.
- An anterior retractor is blunt, sits on the rim, and never slips anteromedial to iliopsoas
- Clearing inferior osteophytes can tear the obturator vessels
- Before removing a protruded cup: CT angiography, abdomen prepped, vascular surgeon ready
- Position the pelvis on the symphysis or ASIS, never on the opposite femoral triangle
